name: fold
one_line: wrap each input line to fit in a given width
plain: `fold` cuts long lines into shorter ones of a fixed width. By default it cuts at 80 characters, even in the middle of a word, unless you ask it to break at spaces.
It is handy for turning one huge line (a Base64 string, a hash list or a key) into neat blocks that you can read, copy or compare.
when: Wrap a long Base64 or hex string.
Cut a long line into equal pieces.
Make text fit a narrow screen.

examples.title: Wrap at 80 columns
examples.explain: Every output line has at most 80 characters.

examples.title: Break at spaces, not mid-word
examples.explain: -s breaks after the last space before the limit, so words stay whole.

examples.title: Wrap Base64 to the standard 64
examples.explain: PEM and many tools expect 64-character lines.

examples.title: Count bytes, not columns
examples.explain: -b counts bytes instead of display columns, good for non-ASCII text.

examples.title: Split a string into characters
examples.explain: Width 1 puts each character on its own line, which you can then sort or count.

mistakes: Forgetting that fold does not remove existing newlines.
Confusing fold with fmt: fmt reflows paragraphs, fold only chops.
Using fold -w 1 on a very large file and flooding the screen.
try: Take a long hash and fold it at 16 characters.
Fold a paragraph at 50 with and without -s.
Use fold -w 1 on a word and count letters with sort | uniq -c.
see_also: fmt(1), cut(1), base64(1), tr(1), column(1), less(1).
captured_with: Examples are written to explain a technique; they are not captured output.
